items.body: Voters cast their ballots during the May 19, 2026, primary election at The Waterfront in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) This year, Idaho voters have a lot to decide on: Who will be the state’s next governor or U.S. senator? Should two constitutional amendments pass? Should voters pass their own law to repeal the state’s abortion ban? 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More But in the mix is a poll that the Idaho Legislature called for: What should be the state’s official gun? Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. The state Legislature considered a bill this year to allow members of the public to carry concealed guns inside parts of courthouses that aren’t meant for court, like offices for county commissioners and clerks. The advisory question on the ballot this year asks voters to weigh in on the Legislature’s possible decision to declare a firearm — out of a mix of well-known Western and American guns — as Idaho’s official state gun. If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. Ten other states have declared state guns , according to the National Rifle Association, a prominent gun lobbying group. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho lawmaker hopes the advisory question will boost voter turnout One of the lawmakers behind the push for the ballot question, Rep. Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said he thought it might drum up voter turnout during a year when many consequential issues are on the ballot. In election years when the president isn’t on the ballot, like this year, fewer voters tend to participate. “Voter turnout is always important,” he said in an interview. “… When you have a lot of voter apathy, I think we don’t get as good of results as we could if we had an informed electorate that was actually out and voting.” The votes won’t be the final say. “The results,” the bill says, “will guide the Legislature as to which gun shall be designated the state gun of Idaho.” Idaho Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, and Idaho House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, walk Gov. Brad Little out of the House chambers after the governor delivered his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) But Monks said this is the only time he knows of when the state sought public input before designating a state item. Monks acknowledges that not everyone loves the idea of declaring a state gun. “I don’t think you can make everybody always happy. The majority of people in Idaho do have guns,” he said. “We have a pretty high percentage of gun ownership in our state. And so I think it reflects the fact that Idaho is a very gun-friendly state, and that it is an important part of our culture in many aspects.” He stressed that the push for the ballot question didn’t take much time. “I had some people ask me, ‘How come this is your priority?’ I’m like, ‘Well, this isn’t my priority. It’s just something we did kind of on the side,’” Monks said. “I put in 12 to 14 hour days there all the time, and I can tell you I spent very little time on this particular issue. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in
items.body: U.S. Attorney for the District of Idaho Bart Davis in his Boise office. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said. “I am unable to overstate the privilege it has been to work with the dedicated and remarkable women and men of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Davis said in a written statement. “These great lawyers and support staff faithfully enforce the law, work to keep Idaho and our country safe, support our law enforcement partners and protect the civil rights of others. I am proud of the work they do every day.” President Donald Trump nominated Davis for U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho last year, and the U.S. Senate confirmed Davis on Oct. 7, 2025 – exactly one year before Davis announced his retirement. Davis previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho from 2017 to 2021 during Trump’s first term. Prior to serving as U.S. attorney, Davis practiced law in Idaho Falls and served in the Idaho Senate for 19 years. Davis, a Republican, served as Senate majority leader for 15 years, where he was regarded as a powerful and intelligent legislative leader. “Bart Davis has served the State of Idaho and our country with distinction throughout a remarkable career,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a written statement. “His sound legal judgment, deep knowledge of Idaho and unwavering commitment to doing what is right have been invaluable to our state.” Davis also served as co-chairman of the 2021 Idaho Commission for Reapportionment , which was charged with redrawing Idaho’s congressional and legislative boundaries following the 2020 census to ensure political representation is proportional. During a 2025 interview with the Idaho Capital Sun, Davis called serving as U.S. attorney, “the best job I ever had.” “… to work with these people who are genuinely trying to even-handedly apply the laws of the United States of America,” Davis said. “It impressed me then, and it impresses me now.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Governor says Davis strengthened relationship between Justice Department and Idaho Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in Idaho, defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States, the office said. In the past year under Davis’ leadership, the office said it has filed 298 criminal charges, including 103 drug trafficking cases, 89 violent crimes cases, 69 immigration cases and 22 fraud cases. “During his time as U.S. Attorney for Idaho, Bart strengthened the relationship between Idaho and the U.S. Department of Justice and represented our state with integrity and professionalism,” Little said. “ We will miss his counsel, his wisdom and his steady leadership. I am grateful for Bart’s many years of service and friendship, and I wish him all the best as he enters retirement and has more time to enjoy with his wife, children and grandchildren.” Davis and his wife, Marion, have six children and 14 grandchildren. Davis and Marion recently celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.summary: Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, left, and Independent Leadership Council co-founder Adam Brandon speak about Achilles' commitment to not caucus with either major party, to only serve two terms, hold public town halls and participate in debates if elected. Achilles held the press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun)
items.body: Independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles, left, and Independent Leadership Council co-founder Adam Brandon speak about Achilles' commitment to not caucus with either major party, to only serve two terms, hold public town halls and participate in debates if elected. Achilles held the press conference on Oct. 7, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho independent U.S. Senate candidate Todd Achilles on Wednesday pledged to not caucus with either party if he’s elected. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Achilles, who served in the Idaho Legislature as a Democrat before announcing his independent run for U.S. Senate, is running against incumbent Republican Sen. Jim Risch , who’s in his 18th year as a senator. Achilles was joined at the Idaho state Capitol in Boise by Adam Brandon, the co-founder of a national advocacy organization promoting independent candidates called the Independent Leadership Council . Achilles also committed to serve a maximum of two terms, hold town halls in each of Idaho’s 44 counties every two years, and to engage in public debates. Brandon previously was president of FreedomWorks, which helped tea party candidates get elected to office. That organization dissolved in 2024 , Politico reported. “Every vote that he casts, both parties are going to have to come to him for his vote to represent the state of Idaho, and I think that is incredibly, incredibly powerful,” Brandon said. Idaho US Senate candidates weigh in on tariffs, Iran War, federal spending and more In the letter Achilles signed to make these commitments, he said the U.S. Senate rules would still guarantee him a committee seat despite not caucusing with the major parties. The two independent U.S. senators — Angus King of Maine and Bernie Sanders of Vermont — both caucus with Senate Democrats. When King won his election in 2012, he announced he would caucus with the Democrats because it would allow him to participate more in the committee process, PBS News reported at the time. Committee assignments are largely decided by party leaders and then formally voted on by the entire Senate. During the event, Achilles also signed a sworn, notarized statement that would resign him from office in 2039 — meaning if elected, he would only be able to serve two, six-year terms. A spokesman for the Achilles campaign said the letter will be sent to either the governor’s office or secretary of state to keep. “We’re serious about this,” Achilles said Wednesday. “That’s it. I don’t want to spend more than 12 years in D.C. I love Idaho’s mountains. I want to get back here and get my skis on and do what I love doing. So two terms. That’s it.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: Hundreds of Idahoans gathered in the rotunda of the Idaho Capitol on Jan. 12, 2026, to protest proposed cuts to the state's Medicaid program. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it. Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work. Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. Then what? Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. These are Idahoans who already qualified for Medicaid, including people whose serious medical conditions should qualify them for a medical frailty exemption. Administrative red tape should not become another obstacle between a cancer patient and the care they need. When that happens, the consequences aren’t limited to the patient. Their families suffer too and local care providers must then care for somebody with no ability to pay the bill. It’s a terrible scenario and one Medicaid expansion has prevented from being widescale. This past session, House Bill 913 established the Jan. 1 start date for federally mandated work requirements. Medicaid proponents had requested a one-year extension to give the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and our residents more time to learn about the changes and implementation. That did not happen, so we hope Idaho lawmakers grasp fully their responsibility to hold true to the promises they made clearly and often during all those Boise debates over work requirements. Then, they were firm in their convictions that no eligible person would ever be stripped of healthcare. Policymakers should be just as committed now to making work requirement exemptions clear and accessible as they were about putting them into law. Coverage losses from work requirements usually aren’t because someone suddenly became ineligible, but because eligible people get caught in paperwork, reporting requirements, missed notices or other government bureaucracy. Officials with the League of Women Voters of Idaho said Little did not respond to their invitation to participate in the forum, though they left an empty chair open for him on the stage at South Junior High School in Boise in case he decided to participate. Pickens, a trial attorney and small business owner, said her first action if she is elected governor will be to present a state budget that restores the tax revenue and many of the budget cuts that Little and the Idaho Legislature cut during the 2026 legislative session. “It’s going to restore mental health funding,” Pickens said. “It’s going to restore Medicaid expansion. It’s going to restore full funding for public education, and that is critically important because the one thing I’ve heard across this state is Idaho families and the Idaho working class are hurting.” 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More Stegner, a retired Idaho Supreme Court justice, said his first action in office as governor would be to repeal the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit, which Little signed into law as House Bill 93 in 2025. “I think my first executive action would be to try to bring litigation against the vouchers as best I could,” Stegener said. “I continue to believe that it’s unconstitutional that we are funding private school students and homeschool students when we’re not adequately funding our own public school students,” Stegner added. John Stegner is running for governor in 2026. (Photo courtesy of John Stegner) Little, Pickens, Stegner, Libertarian Paul Sand, a Constitution Party candidate who legally changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life and independent write-in candidate named Jacob Burnett are all running for governor in the Nov. 3 general election. Tuesday’s candidate forum lasted 90 minutes and featured a question-and-answer format, with some questions submitted by audience members in attendance and others written by event organizers. “This is not a debate, it is a forum, an exchange of ideas, related to the issues confronting our beautiful state of Idaho,” League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid said at the beginning of Tuesday’s forum. House Joint Resolution 6 would amend the Idaho Constitution to make English the official language of Idaho. items.title: Passing HJR 4 would give Idaho Legislature sole authority to legalize marijuana, other drugs
items.summary: A voter casts his ballot in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dat
items.body: A voter casts his ballot in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idahoans voting in November’s general election will decide whether to give the Idaho Legislature the sole power to regulate marijuana and other drugs — and eliminate their right to bring a citizen-led ballot initiative to do so. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. House Joint Resolution 4 is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank) As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet. Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank , she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit. “People who need diapers need our help,” she said. There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting. “Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives. Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian , one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers. “SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said. Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.” Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors. “We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.” The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month. “This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.” As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges. “The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said. “Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.” One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives. “Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. It’s pretty incredible to watch.” The Idaho Diaper Bank is living up to its slogan, “Changing Babies. Changing Lives.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: The rotunda of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) When two mental health clinic owners in Idaho set out to restore critical services for people with severe mental illness, they faced an uphill battle. The Idaho Legislature was gearing up for across-the-board budget cuts. But Laura Scuri and Ric Boyce armed lawmakers with information and data — and spent time talking to journalists when four patients died after the mobile treatment service had been cut. Ric Boyce, director of Mental Health Specialists, testifies before the Idaho Legislature’s Medicaid Review Panel on Dec. 15, 2025 in Rexburg. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The two often worked behind the scenes, directly with lawmakers instead of testifying before committees. “We formed individual relationships with half the Legislature pretty much,” Boyce recalled in an interview. In the end, the programs that they advocated served as a rare instance of a budget cut that state lawmakers reversed. On the final day of this year’s legislative session, Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed into law a bill that temporarily restored funding for the programs that the two providers pushed for: the Assertive Community Treatment program, a mobile program for people with severe mental illness, and peer support services, which helps people navigate treatment. After four patients died, Idaho governor approves restoring cut Medicaid mental health programs Now, a mental health nonprofit plans to honor the two. This week, the National Alliance on Mental Illness of Idaho plans to award them both the Kathie Garrett Impact Award, named after a former Idaho lawmaker. In a news release, the nonprofit said the duo’s advocacy “led to the return of those programs.” The award came as a surprise. “I don’t think either one of us were thinking for a second it’s something that would be noticed,” said Boyce, a clinical social worker who owns Mental Health Specialists, a clinic in eastern Idaho’s Chubbuck. “What was important to us was that we were able to get the clients we were working with back into the program they needed so badly. And that was enough.” Scuri, who co-owns Access Behavioral Health Services in Boise, said it’s her first award. “So it’s extra special to me — especially with the environment that we’re in, and all the changes,” she said. But he said this experience tested that conception. “What I learned was that there are ways to make change happen even when it seems hopeless,” he said. While he and Scuri were talking with lawmakers, he said they also found lawmakers coming to them for answers — to questions raised by community members in letters and direct outreach on all sorts of Medicaid changes, not just the cuts they were focused on. “Even individual advocacy, of sending a single letter, cumulatively had an effect. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Two days after a grand jury indicted a former Idaho state government employee on two felony counts of misuse of public funds, a local judge dismissed the case — after a request from the prosecutor. The case marked the first criminal charges — and a rare public update — to emerge from a yearslong investigation launched by Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador that probed how the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare doled out $72 million in federal child care grants in 2021 and 2022. The official who was criminally charged, Ericka Rupp, oversaw the grant program. In the indictment, filed in Canyon County District Court last week, the grand jury charged Rupp with two felony counts of misuse of public funds and securities, for allegedly illegally authorizing, appropriating or otherwise misusing more than $300 of the government’s money. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador speaks at the Idaho Medal of Honor ceremony held Sept. 1, 2026, at the Idaho Statehouse in Boise. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office) Labrador’s special prosecutor, Canyon County Prosecuting Attorney Christopher Boyd, told the Idaho Capital Sun that the amount of money allegedly misused was not specified in the indictment, but that it would’ve been an issue to determine during a potential trial. Boyd said he moved to drop the indictment based on feedback from jurors. “I, however, asked of them whether they felt the case was one worth pursuing in terms of resources,” Boyd wrote in a text message. “I truly wanted their opinion on this. They had spent several full days taking testimony. The majority of jurors felt my time was better spent focusing on the many other serious crimes they worked on.” For each count, the penalties could have been up to 14 years imprisonment and up to $10,000 in fines, according to state laws cited in the indictment. Rupp’s attorney, Scott McKay, declined to comment. In a Friday order, Third District Judge Thomas W. Whitney wrote he was dismissing the case upon the state’s request. The court hasn’t released records supporting the judge’s decision to dismiss the case. Special prosecutor Christopher Boyd argues in district court that the Idaho Office of the Attorney General should not pay legal fees associated with litigation that set to block the office’s civil subpoena. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Pending permission from the court, Boyd said he hopes to release a report with more details in the coming days. Asked whether he’d pursue charges against Rupp, or other people linked to the investigation, Boyd said: “The report should conclude my investigation.” The Idaho attorney general’s office could not immediately be reached for comment. Department of Health and Welfare spokesperson Greg Stahl directed questions about the case to parties involved. “(The Department of Health and Welfare) takes seriously its responsibility to be a good steward of taxpayer dollars and remains committed to transparency, accountability, and the appropriate use of public funds,” Stahl said in a statement. The race, she said, comes down to “who’s the best attorney to be the chief legal officer for the state of Idaho.” “I’m trying to restore the tradition of sound legal advice, regardless of who the clients are or their political affiliations,” Hickman said at a news conference announcing the endorsements. “So I’m running as a Democrat because my opponent’s a Republican.” Democratic candidate for Idaho attorney general Lori Hickman stands in front of more than a dozen deputy attorneys general, and two former Republican AGs, who endorsed her in the 2026 election. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) Hickman stood outside the old Ada County Courthouse across the street from the Idaho State Capitol, beside a pool of attorneys who she said collectively have hundreds of years of experience. Hickman is an Idaho attorney with two decades of experience, including at global tech company Micron, and has served as board chair of Mormon Women for Ethical Government. Labrador is a former Idaho congressman and an immigration attorney. He became the state’s attorney general in 2023, after defeating the state’s longest-serving attorney general, Lawrence Wasden, in the Republican primary election. Wasden was among the pack endorsing Hickman. At the press conference, he and former Idaho Republican Attorney General Jim Jones, who also served as a state Supreme Court justice, cheered by her side. In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. Idaho’s last Democratic attorney general was Larry Echohawk in 1995. In a statement, the Labrador campaign seemed unsurprised by the endorsements. “Lawrence Wasden, Jim Jones, and disgruntled former employees. items.body: State Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, asks a question during the March 16, 2026, Idaho House Local Government Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) An incumbent Boise state representative who lives in a competitive legislative district has raised the most money of any candidate for the Idaho Legislature in 2026, online state campaign finance records show. Rep. Steve Berch, D-Boise, has raised $212,580.79 as of Tuesday afternoon. Although Republicans control a supermajority in the Idaho Legislature, Berch is the only candidate in Idaho’s 105 legislative districts who has raised more than $200,000 this year. Search Idaho campaign finance records online To search through finance records for each Idaho candidate, go to Idaho Sunshine, the Idaho Secretary of State’s campaign finance website . Through Idaho Sunshine, the public can search for candidates, political action committees, campaign expenditures, campaign contributions, reports and more. Berch also raised the most money heading into this year’s primary elections , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. In an interview Tuesday, Berch attributed his fundraising success to engaging directly with voters and knocking on tens of thousands of doors in his legislative district. “It’s really very humbling, and it tells me that people like what I’m doing in terms of knocking on doors, holding in-person town hall meetings and sending out very detailed newsletters so they know the reason why I vote the way I do,” Berch said. Most of Berch’s campaign contributions came from people and from within Idaho. According to online state campaign finance reports, Berch raised $153,816 from people, $27,450 from companies, $9,000 from political committees and $1,000 from Democratic central committees. Berch raised $169,226 in Idaho and $22,040 from out-of-state donors, records show. The rest of Berch’s campaign money was un-itemized. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More Berch represents District 15 in west Boise, which has flipped back and forth between Democratic and Republican control since at least 2018. Berch’s opponent in the Nov. 3 general election, Republican Steve Keyser, has reported raising $13,592.67. District 15 is one of the rare truly split legislative districts in Idaho. For the past two years, Berch held one of the legislative seats in District 15 while Republicans held the other two. Two years before, Berch and the Democrats controlled two of the district’s seats while Republicans held just one. For that reason, both Republicans and Democrats will be looking to pick up a seat in District 15 in November’s general election What other Idaho legislative candidates are raising the most money Among the 10 Idaho legislative candidates who raised the most campaign money in 2026, seven are Republicans and three are Democrats. In total, six candidates have reported raising more than $100,000 in campaign money this year. Although it was decided months ago, Idaho’s primary election appears to have played a big role in campaign fundraising this year. Two candidates from the Republican primary election for Idaho Senate District 1, Sen. Jim Woodward and former Sen. Scott Herndon, were among the top four legislative candidates in terms of campaign fundraising for 2026. Herndon won the primary in May and advanced to the Nov. 3 general election, where he is running against independent candidate Steve Johnson. Legislative leadership positions also may have played a role in campaign fundraising this year. Some of the Idaho Legislature’s top ranking members, including House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star; Senate President Pro Tem Kelly Anthon, R-Rupert; and Senate Minority Leader Melissa Wintrow, D-Boise, all made the top 10 list for fundraising for legislative candidates this year. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Three out of four candidates running to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate discussed their differing approaches on tariffs, military actions, immigration, and more Wednesday night in Caldwell. The race’s incumbent, Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, declined to participate. Independents Todd Achilles and Natalie Fleming, and Libertarian Matt Loesby, spoke at the forum hosted by the League of Women Voters, Caldwell Chamber of Commerce and the local American Association of University Women at Caldwell City Hall. 2026 Voter Guide The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote. Read More The three candidates differed in their proposals to address the federal budget deficit, reform immigration, and rein in military action abroad. Risch’s campaign manager Marc Kilmer told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that Risch didn’t participate because, “It was organized by someone who has publicly endorsed our opponent, and therefore we felt it would not be an impartial debate.” Kilmer said the endorsement came from former Idaho Republican state Rep. Julie Yamamoto of Caldwell, but it wasn’t clear how she was connected to the organizers. He couldn’t immediately be reached to clarify. League of Women Voters of Idaho President Jean Henscheid told the Sun she didn’t know of any organizers that endorsed a candidate in the race. To watch the entire forum, visit the City of Caldwell Youtube page . How would the candidates address the high cost of living and tariffs? All of the candidates agreed that the existing 50% tariff on a range of Canadian good s, should be rolled back and implemented more strategically. Achilles argued that Congress needed to “take back control” of tariff policy from the White House, and manage them in a “more strategic way” to protect domestic industries. “Congress needs to stand up and be an independent branch of government, and execute their constitutional duties, which is to be in control of tariffs,” he said. Loesby argued that tariffs were a small part of the problem when it came to addressing high costs of living for Americans. He agreed that the existing high tariffs should be rolled back and the taxes on imported products should be used to address trade imbalances with China. To address cost of living challenges, he said the U.S. needed to “end all these horrific foreign wars,” and “deport the millions of people who should not be in our country” to address housing costs. Fleming called the trade war with Canada, who imposed retaliatory tariffs against the U.S., “mind-boggling,” and said the import taxes should be rolled back. To address the high cost of living, she argued that the immigration systems should be reformed so immigrant workers can more easily work in the U.S. legally. “We all know that we have some wonderful immigrants who are building our homes and are providing food for us,” Fleming said. “And so we need to streamline the immigration process for them.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. The treasurer’s office serves as the state’s chief financial officer — which includes overseeing the receipt of state money, accounting for disbursement of funds, investing idle state money, and administering the unclaimed property program , the 529 College Savings Fund, and the Idaho ABLE savings accounts. He previously ran Boise-based Harmonic Investment Advisors. He is a longtime institutional portfolio manager and a chartered financial analyst, which is an internationally recognized professional certification for advanced investment management and financial analysis, he said. “I’m a very logical individual, and I’m also a former college golfer, so I’ve spent my entire life competing, where numbers matter more than how someone dresses, what party they’re in, and so forth,” Jones said. “… You either post the score on the golf course, or you don’t. She has been a public school teacher, and a mediator and business consultant. She said she wants to run again because her work has helped the state. “I think I’m doing a good job, and I can see that it elevates Idahoans,” Ellsworth said. “It’s very uplifting. The state’s IDLE fund is used to balance cash flow and is used to ensure there is adequate money for state appropriation. Money that isn’t being spent right away can be invested “at the best rate possible at the safest level of risk,” according to the treasurer’s website. (Shelby Wyatt/Source NM) An Idaho judge dismissed a lawsuit from a Boise daycare and parents that sought to block enforcement of a state law that bans daycares from requiring vaccines or medical treatment. The lawsuit claimed that the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, arguing its language bans a range of routine health protections — including handwashing and sending home sick kids. But last week, Chief U.S. District Judge for the District of Idaho Amanda K. Brailsford granted Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, which was brought by Le Soleil Child Care LLC, and three parents whose kids attend the daycare or hope to. In her ruling, the federal judge wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” “The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote, ruling that the daycare didn’t show that the state law was unconstitutionally vague. “The Court agrees with the AG that Le Soleil is free to promote its beliefs and values about public health and vaccinations …” the judge wrote. “The only thing the (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) prevents is Le Soleil requiring that only vaccinated students hear those values.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE AG praises court ruling. Parents, daycare consider appealing, lawyer says. The ruling upholds a state law that bans daycares, businesses, governments and schools from mandating vaccines or “medical interventions,” which are defined as: “a medical procedure, treatment, device, drug injection, medication, or medical action taken to diagnose, prevent, or cure a disease or alter the health or biological function of a person.” In a statement, Labrador said he was pleased with the court’s decision. “Parents make medical decisions for their children. A daycare does not,” Labrador said in a statement . “The Legislature protected that choice in the Medical Freedom Act, and the court upheld it. Daycares can tell parents what they believe about vaccines and health, but they cannot turn a child away because of a parent’s medical decision. That decision belongs to families, and I’m pleased the court agreed.” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US Idaho has the lowest rate of kindergartners — nearly four out of every five — who are reportedly up to date on their measles vaccine, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data . The state has reported 10 measles cases this year, as nearby states experience outbreaks. In a statement, Andrea Carone, an attorney for the daycare and parents who sued, wrote that the plaintiffs are considering appealing to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. “Our clients are obviously disappointed by the district court’s ruling and the narrow manner in which it interpreted the right at issue,” Carone said. “The Idaho Medical Freedom Act places parents like our individual clients and daycares like Le Soleil in the untenable position of being unable to take reasonable steps to protect their children or children in their care from childhood diseases that vaccines shield against. items.body: A voter casts her ballot during the May 19, 2026, primary election at Westside Elementary School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Ahead of the 2026 general election, Idaho election officials mailed out hundreds of thousands of informational pamphlets to households across the state. The state’s official voter pamphlet has already started to arrive at some households, the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office announced. 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested primaries. Read More The voter pamphlet includes information about the range of questions on the ballot — such as Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would end the state’s abortion ban and establish reproductive rights; a proposed constitutional amendment that would only allow the Legislature to legalize drugs, such as marijuana; a constitutional amendment that would declare English as the state’s official language; and an advisory question that solicits a public vote to declare a state gun. That’s along with information about key upcoming election dates, voting options and voter registration. (You can also find information about those issues, along with races for statewide constitutional offices and in select legislative districts, in the Idaho Capital Sun’s voter guide .) “Election season is underway,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican running for re-election, said in a statement. “Every household in Idaho can expect to receive a Voter Pamphlet with the information you need to be ready to vote in November. This special America 250 edition includes some fun nods to our history as we celebrate 250 years of America and make our mark on the future of our state. Make a plan, get registered, and vote!” To view the pamphlet online and access it in Spanish or an audio format, visit VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. That’s also where voters can see what their ballot will look like, along with other election resources. The voter pamphlet does not include information about candidates. In 2023 and 2024, the Idaho Legislature did not approve McGrane’s proposed bill to replace the voter pamphlet with a voter guide, which would include information about candidates. According to a 2024 poll in Boise State University’s Idaho Public Policy Survey, 78% of Idahoans favored a state-issued voter guide. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

(Photo by Jordan Gale/Oregon Capital Chronicle) A new data center campus could soon be coming to federal land near Hermiston in eastern Oregon. It would be the first in Oregon sited on federal public land, and one of at least 12 proposed for more than 17,500 Bureau of Land Management acres across western states under President Donald Trump’s July 2025 executive order to hasten data center development. The proposals on federal land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming were first reported last week by The Washington Sun, whose reporters reviewed difficult to find right-of-way requests via BLM’s Mineral and Land Records System . The bulk of federally managed land in the U.S. is in the West, including in Oregon where half the state’s land is owned and managed by the federal government. Oregon is among the top 10 markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research. Under the executive order, Trump mandated that federally owned land and resources be used for “the expeditious and orderly development of data centers (…) to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.” It’s the first time the Bureau of Land Management, tasked with managing more than 245 million public acres for uses that include animal grazing, timber harvesting and recreation, has been ordered to include data centers in its portfolio. Several months after Trump issued the order, the California-based energy company Copia, which has an office in Lake Oswego, submitted an application to site the Charlestown Data Center and Battery Energy Storage System in Umatilla County on 106 acres of BLM land. The company most recently submitted a draft plan for development of the data center project on May 8, 2026, available only via federal public records request, according to Sarah Bennett, a spokesperson for the bureau’s Northwest region office. items.body: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright (center) visits Idaho National Laboratory with Idaho Gov. Brad Little (right) in December 2025. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy) Editor’s Note: This is the first installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining the proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focuses on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. The series continues Monday and Tuesday with a closer look at the cases for and against bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Idaho Gov. Brad Little said he will not jeopardize the health of the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer or the health of Idahoans as he continues to negotiate potentially bringing a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. “I’ve had this direct conversation with Secretary (of Energy Chris) Wright: Disposal of spent fuel over the aquifer in Idaho – that’s a nonstarter,” Little said in an interview Wednesday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. In July, U.S. Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho is one of five states selected as a finalist to host one of the new innovation campuses. Little signed a memorandum of understanding in July with the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, to hold formal discussions and negotiations about bringing an innovation campus to Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) If Idaho is selected as a host site, the federal government has said the state will have to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states. A Request for Information Response that Little signed and submitted to the federal government in March describes an accelerated process that takes “months rather than decades” to bring the “initial capabilities” of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027. But on Wednesday, Little said things aren’t moving that quickly. “There’s a long way to go before this happens,” Little said. “(The DOE) would love to identify some sites, and I believe … they may need something by the end of the year. But it will not be in any way, shape or form a final agreement.” Little said the documents he signed do not obligate Idaho to host an innovation campus or accept nuclear fuel or radioactive waste. Instead, the agreements simply bring Idaho to the negotiating table, the governor said. Little said it makes sense for Idaho to be at the negotiating table because of the potential economic benefits to the state, the infrastructure, the experience at Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and the need for additional, reliable energy. The memorandum of understanding lists a Sept. 30 deadline, but Little said he doesn’t think agreements will be reached that quickly, and he suggested the two sides could either continue talks or sign another memorandum of understanding with a later deadline. Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to comment for this series of articles. What is a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus? There are now five other potential host sites for one or more DOE innovation campuses – Utah, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Louisiana and West Virginia. According to the DOE , a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus is “designed to support activities across the full nuclear fuel lifecycle, including fuel fabrication, enrichment, reprocessing used nuclear fuel and final disposition of used nuclear fuel. Depending on state priorities and regional capabilities, the campuses may also host advanced reactor deployment, power generation, advanced manufacturing and co-located data centers.” An innovation campus could bring thousands of jobs and millions or billions of dollars in revenue to the state or states selected to host a campus, supporters and DOE officials have said. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was corrected at 2:08 p.m. on Sept. 24 to clarify the Idaho Innocence Project’s role in Charles Fain’s case. The Idaho Innocence Project helped secure Fain’s certificate of innocence and identify the true perpetrator, but was not involved in his original exoneration. Charles Fain says his three favorite letters in the alphabet are D-N-A. In 2001, Fain was exonerated and released from an Idaho prison after nearly 20 years on death row for a rape and murder he did not commit, using DNA analysis. After his release, the Idaho Innocence Project helped police identify the true perpetrator and got Fain a certificate of innocence and compensation for wrongful conviction. The Idaho Innocence Project has been shuttered for more than two years because of a lack of funding. However, on Sept. 17, Fain joined Innocence Project founder Greg Hampikian and fellow exoneree Amanda Knox to usher in a new group continuing the work of overturning wrongful convictions. Hampikian lent his DNA expertise to Knox’s defense team to help free her from an Italian prison. (Photo by G Kenny3 Photography) Knox sits on the board of The Innocence Center , a nonprofit, free law firm based in San Diego that will take on cases in Idaho to try and free wrongfully convicted inmates. Hampikian, a forensic DNA expert, also lent his expertise to Knox’s defense team in the highly publicized case and helped free her from an Italian prison after she was wrongfully sentenced for the murder of her roommate while studying abroad. “It would be a desperate situation if these projects didn’t exist,” Knox said in an interview last week in Boise. “And when I heard that the Idaho Innocence Project was shutting down, I was really, really worried for the state of Idaho, because who else is going to do it?” The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik was admitted to the Idaho bar on Sept. 18 so that he may work as an attorney for these cases in Idaho. “We’re committed to making this happen and making sure that wherever there are innocent people in prison, there’s an organization to support them,” Semanchik told a small gathering last week to kickoff the new work. Hampikian said he personally selected The Innocence Center to take up the work. “My last great act, after 20 years of the Innocence Project, was to choose a successor,” Hampikian said. “… (Semanchik) said, ‘I’ll get barred in Idaho, and I’ll take the cases until we raise the money.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, this guy’s got skin in the game.’” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force meets on Sept. 23, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) A group of rural Idaho hospital leaders, state officials and tribal representatives met for the first time Wednesday to oversee the process of awarding nearly $190 million in federal rural health grants. The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force received an update on the state’s administration of the federal Rural Health Transformation grant program — a nationwide $50 billion, five-year federal grant Congress approved through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare) “We are building and flying the plane at the same time. That feels like it’s been the consistent theme of this,” Idaho Department Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron said Wednesday. The task force is meant to provide input on the process of implementation, help navigate potential challenges, and ensure the state is balancing statewide initiatives with actual needs of rural communities, Charron said. The nearly 20 funding opportunities posted by the state have closed, and Health and Welfare staff are reviewing applications to award subgrants. The opportunities include funding to provide school-based family support, chronic disease prevention and cancer screening, a cognitive care network, and diabetes prevention and management. The agency awarded national nonprofit Comagine Health with a grant to create a collaborative system to improve maternal and child health statewide, according to the program website. The state is nearing an Oct. 30 deadline to award all of the $186 million received for the first year of the program. “It is going to be a very, very tight timeline coming up to the end,” Charron said. For a health provider infrastructure opportunity, which will be about $97 million of the total grant, Charron said the agency received more than 250 applications asking for a total of more than $300 million. “That means that we will have to say no to some,” she said. Idaho submitted its first required report to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, which is overseeing the program, on Aug. 31. The report will help determine how much funding the state gets in the second year of the five-year program. Charron said that the state hasn’t heard feedback on that report yet. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s received sightly less funding because of low rural population density When Congress approved the funding, it split the $50 billion into two allocation methods. Half of the money was split equally among all 50 states. The remaining $25 billion was to be distributed based on certain metrics. Idaho’s low population density in rural communities and low density of rural healthcare providers were “challenges” for the scoring criteria, Charron said “Centers for Medicare and Medicaid had very specific criteria to drill down into: What does rural healthcare delivery look like in that specific state? And this is where we were a bit challenged, frankly, because we are so frontier in our state,” she said. Idaho scored highly for its existing state policies that align with Trump administration priorities, Charron said, including commitments to encourage the presidential fitness test in rural schools and changing the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, to ban purchases of candy and soda with it. items.body: Ashley and Joshua Durham used the Affordable Care Act marketplace for their health insurance after they began their family medicine practice in Boise, Idaho, in late 2023. But the couple say they opted out of health insurance for their family of four this year after they saw their ACA premium payments jump to nearly $1,600 a month. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News) This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026. Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance. When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600. Top insurance official recommends task force for studying Idaho’s most critical healthcare issues They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years. “It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.” The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured. But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027. The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments , especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry. Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine , which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers. “The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’” As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans. The number of people without insurance in the U.S. is expected to increase by roughly 15 million over 10 years because of the expiration of the expanded ACA subsidies and $1.1 trillion in estimated cuts resulting from President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the Congressional Budget Office. Healthier people are the most likely to opt out of insurance. That leaves insurance covering a smaller pool of people who tend to be sicker and need more expensive care. items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. A panel of Ninth Circuit judges heard arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit challenging Idaho's abortion ban, seeking expanded exemptions. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) A panel of federal appeals judges will soon decide whether to continue to allow full enforcement of Idaho’s abortion bans, or to allow a lower court’s previous ruling that provided more exemptions to the law. U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw, Marsha Berzon and Consuelo Callahan heard oral arguments in a virtual hearing Tuesday afternoon. The state of Idaho, represented by an attorney from the conservative Christian legal advocacy group Alliance Defending Freedom , argued that the laws should be fully enforced as written. Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. ADF attorney Mathew Hoffmann argued that a lower court’s previous ruling that would’ve expanded exemptions to apply to serious health and mental health risks to the mother, was not grounded in historical precedent. He said there is no right to “therapeutic” abortions. Attorneys representing Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb argued that an earlier court decision from U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill should go back into effect. The ruling would’ve prevented the Ada County prosecutor and Idaho attorney general from enforcing Idaho’s abortion ban in cases where the mother’s health faced serious risk or her life was at risk due to self harm. Winmill later narrowed this block on enforcement to only protect abortions performed by Seyb. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador. (Photo courtesy of Attorney General Raúl Labrador) After Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed, a Ninth Circuit panel placed a hold on Winmill’s order, and the law went back into effect. Hoffmann said Winmill’s decision expanding the exemptions created “an abortion-on-demand regime.” “They leave it up to the subjective judgment of doctors to determine a risk sufficient to justify abortion,” he said. Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, argued on behalf of Seyb that the expanded exemptions to the law were necessary. “The injunction entered by the district court in this case is narrow. It would enable only a small number of patients each year to obtain an abortion,” Toti said. “But for those patients, access to that care is vitally important, as the district court found.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Hoffmann argued that it would not, because the Constitution does not explicitly provide a right to abortions. Toti argued that the 2022 decision did not mention rights to life and health, which she said are violated by the Idaho ban’s limited exemptions. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for fr
items.body: The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse. The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law and Boise State University’s Institute for Advancing American Values , according to a Secretary of State’s Office press release. The keynote speaker for the event will be Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who has championed Disagree Better, a national, nonpartisan initiative “designed to reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate,” according to its website. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. (Photo courtesy of Phil McGrane) “Free speech is fundamental to our system of government, but protecting it requires more than simply agreeing that it is important,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. “It means listening to people we disagree with, defending their right to speak, and being willing to have difficult conversations. That is what we hope to accomplish with the Idaho Free Speech Summit.” Sessions at the summit will explore First Amendment issues “ranging from campaign finance and campus free speech to the broader challenges of maintaining civil discourse in an increasingly divided political environment,” the press release said. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (left) listens as Gov. Spencer Cox holds a press conference to present his budget proposal at the Salt Lake County Library in Kearns, Utah, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Cox will talk about how Americans can disagree without abandoning strongly held beliefs, a theme he explores in his new book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt,” according to the release. “We are pleased to be part of a discussion centered on one of our nation’s most important constitutional freedoms,” said Brian Kane, University of Idaho College of Law dean, in the release. “The University of Idaho College of Law is a natural partner for this conversation. Law schools should be places where difficult constitutional questions are examined carefully and where people learn how to engage seriously with ideas they may not share.” The daylong summit will have presentations and panel discussions, followed by an evening reception. A continuing legal education credit will also be available for participating attorneys. “Universities have an important role to play in creating spaces where people can wrestle with difficult questions and hear perspectives different from their own,” said Boise State University’s Andrew Finstuen in the release. “The Summit provides an opportunity to model the kind of thoughtful, constructive dialogue that is essential to a healthy civic culture.” Registration and additional information, including the Summit schedule and speaker lineup, are available at FreeSpeechIdaho.com . “Our goal isn’t to bring together people who all agree,” McGrane said in the release. “It is to bring together people who recognize that our constitutional freedoms are strongest when we defend the right of others to speak, listen to one another, and engage in good faith.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images) With less than two months before the 2026 midterm elections, election officials across Idaho mailed the first round of mail-in ballots to voters who are overseas or who requested absentee ballots locally. The finalization of ballots in Idaho follows after a weekslong crunch to change contested language for an abortion legalization ballot initiative and attempts by the Trump administration to implement a federal rule that could’ve made last-minute changes to ballots. Idaho election officials worry about mail-in ballot changes proposed by Trump administration “Everything is on track,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official who’s running for re-election as a Republican. More than a month before the Nov. 3 general election, local election officials are expected to finalize ballots. That’s because federal law requires the first slate of mail-in ballots be shipped 45 days before federal elections to voters who are overseas, such as members of the military or missionaries. In Ada County, Idaho’s largest, election officials were expecting to mail out more than 24,000 ballots on Friday, Trent Tripple, the Republican county clerk, told the Idaho Capital Sun. That includes overseas and military voters, along with everyone who had already requested an absentee ballot, he said. Voters still have more than a month to request absentee ballots or register to vote before Election Day. Oct. 23 is the deadline to request absentee ballots or pre-register to vote, according to an election calendar on VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. This year, all statewide constitutional offices — such as governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general — are up for election as well as all 105 seats in the Idaho Legislature. Three of Idaho’s four congressional seats will also be on the ballot. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: The Columbia Princess Ferry stays on the Gifford side of the Columbia River as the Modrite Fire exhibits extreme fire behavior just south of Inchelium, Washington. Fires in the state hit tribes particularly hard this year. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information) Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior. Now it’s gone. Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said. “I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.” Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen. Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires. “What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel , executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert. An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks. Nighttime view of the Kaiser Canyon Fire during firing operations on Whitmore Mountain. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information) This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service. The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires. Many residents didn’t have home insurance because the housing didn’t qualify or they couldn’t afford it, said Cindy Marchand, chairwoman of the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, adding that about half of homes destroyed in the fires weren’t insured. Other residents couldn’t afford to upgrade to more fire-resistant material, she said. “The rates are just astronomical in the sense that a lot of people in our area are not able to afford this,” Marchand said. “We have elders living on a single income, they’re on a fixed income, and so they’re having a hard time making it as it is.” By mid-September, the total acres burned across the state reached roughly 900,000 acres, the worst since 2015. Since July, about 200,000 acres burned across the Colville Reservation alone, with the Kaiser Canyon Fire scorching over 138,000 acres and the Modrite fire burning more than 57,000 acres. In Oregon, over 60,000 acres burned across the reservation of the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, where at least six homes were destroyed. The Wrights Spring Fire in Oregon burned through 55,000 acres across Klamath County, national forest and tribal lands. items.body: The Kuna Lions Club is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. (Photo by Getty Images) Here’s something that you should not pass up. The Kuna Lions (my club) is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. The vision and hearing screening will be conducted by Envision , and Terry Reilly Health Services will be doing the diabetes testing. People living in surrounding communities are cordially invited. If there were a poster boy for diabetes screening, it would be me. This has been a summer of amputations – one toe on my right foot and two partial toe amputations on my left foot. I have not been able to do summer activities that I enjoy, such as daily walks around the neighborhood and golf. Yes, these amputations were the result of diabetes. On the bright side, losing a couple of toes is a lot better than losing a foot or a leg. But there’s more to my diabetes story. Twenty-two years ago, I had a five-way heart bypass surgery – which has given me more than two decades of quality living. But veins from that surgery don’t last forever, and some of mine have shown signs of wear. In football terms, I may be getting close to the two minute warning. But as fans know so well, a lot can happen in those last two minutes. I have a great life, and it isn’t done yet. I might have been spared from some of these health challenges if I had diabetes screening 30 years ago. Instead, I ignored some of the obvious symptoms. Recently, I had a chat with Dr. Stuart Black with Terry Reilly Health Services, and he knows all about the importance of the screening. “Some studies show that 10 percent of the population, and as high as 13 percent have diabetes and maybe a fourth of the people with diabetes don’t know about it,” he said. “If screening shows an indication of prediabetes, people can get the care they need and prevent the complications that come with the disease, such as heart disease and kidney problems. Diabetes also is one of the leading causes for blindness.” Dr. Black says that random glucose readings at a screening event may not paint the true picture. For instance, numbers may be on the high side for those who had something to eat before the screening. But high numbers are worth watching. “The more information that a person has, the better,” he says. “I think there are people who are afraid to find out they have diabetes, because they think it’s a death sentence. But that’s not the case. There are great options to help control blood sugars if you have diabetes or prediabetes.” Terry Reilly’s service doesn’t stop with the screening. It’s also a resource, and a relatively affordable one, for those who show signs of prediabetes or diabetes. Terry Reilly Health Services, based in Nampa, has other area clinics – including one in Melba. “We have physicians and clinical pharmacists who are well versed in dealing with diabetes,” Dr. Black said. “Our doors are open to help anyone who is diagnosed, or at risk, for diabetes or prediabetes.” Of course, he says, there are steps people can take without a doctor’s help. “Getting 150 minutes of exercise in a week; eating a healthy diet that focuses more on fruits, vegetables and less on fast foods or processed foods; getting enough sleep; decreasing stress in your life,” he said. “All those things are basic lifestyle choices that people can take, with or without diabetes.” I wish I had followed that advice 30 years ago.
